title: Letters From Please, Sorry and Tomorrow

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ض and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: write ف and ق once each, and name them.
Now say من فضلك (min faḍlik), "please". You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
ض — ḍād, a heavy d.

It is inside من فضلك (min faḍlik), "please". It is ص (ṣād), which you already write, with one dot above. Arabic is sometimes called the language of the ḍād, because the sound is so rare in other languages.
1. start here: close the oval clockwise from its lower-left junction.
2. turn left and rise into the short shoulder without lifting.
3. lift, restart at the baseline junction, and sweep through the trailing bowl.
4. lift again, then place the upper dot last — and only now lift.
Pen lifts: 2.

Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Introduction to Arabic: Egyptian Arabic for first-year students, Alphabet: س ش ص ض (ḍād), independent Daad at 00:43.1–00:46.3 (University of Oregon Libraries Open Textbook, 2023).

segments.instruction: at من فضلك and point at ض (ḍād) inside it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at **من فضلك** and point at ض inside it]

segments.instruction: ض (ḍād) three times, saying ḍ as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: ض three times, saying *ḍ* as you finish each one]
[YOU WRITE: ق, then ض, from memory]

segments.text: Which letter is this — ض? (ḍād, ḍ.) Which word did it come from? (من فضلك, min faḍlik, "please".)

lessons.title: آ (alif madda) — the alif that opens آسف
lessons.gloss: alif madda — the alif that opens آسف

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: آ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: write ق and ض (ḍād) once each, and name them.
Now say آسف (āsif), "sorry". You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
آ (alif madda) — alif with a madda, a long ā at the start of a word.
It opens آسف (āsif), "sorry". The wavy stroke on top, the madda, stretches the vowel: where a plain ا at the start of a word needs a hamza to say a, آ (alif madda) says a long ā.
Put your pen on آ (alif madda) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start this character or which way to travel. It is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.instruction: at آسف and point at آ (alif madda) inside it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at **آسف** and point at آ inside it]

segments.instruction: آ (alif madda) three times, saying ā as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: آ three times, saying *ā* as you finish each one]

segments.instruction: ض (ḍād), then آ (alif madda), from memory
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: ض, then آ, from memory]

segments.text: Which letter is this — آ? (alif madda, ā.) Which word did it come from? (آسف, āsif, "sorry".)

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ز and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: write ض (ḍād) and آ (alif madda) once each, and name them.
Now say أزرق (azraq), "blue". You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
ز — zāy, the sound z.
It is inside أزرق (azraq), "blue", from أحمر أزرق. It is ر (rāʾ), which you already write, with one dot above, and like ر it never joins to the letter after it.
1. start here: begin at the upper tip and descend through the short stroke.
2. without lifting, sweep left through the lower curve without lifting.
3. lift once, then place the dot above — and only now lift.
Pen lifts: 1.

Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Introduction to Arabic: Egyptian Arabic for first-year students, Alphabet ر ز (zāy) و, independent Zay body followed by its upper dot (University of Oregon Libraries Open Textbook, 2023; accessed 2026-08-23).

segments.instruction: at أزرق and point at ز (zāy) inside it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at **أزرق** and point at ز inside it]

segments.instruction: ز (zāy) three times, saying z as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: ز three times, saying *z* as you finish each one]

segments.instruction: آ (alif madda), then ز (zāy), from memory
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: آ, then ز, from memory]

segments.text: Which letter is this — ز? (zāy, z.) Which word did it come from? (أزرق, azraq, "blue".)

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: غ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: write آ (alif madda) and ز (zāy) once each, and name them.
Now say إلى الغد (ilā l-ghad), "see you tomorrow". You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
غ — ghayn, a gh gargled at the back of the throat.
It is inside إلى الغد (ilā l-ghad), "see you tomorrow". It is ع (ʿayn), which you already write, with one dot above, the third family where a single dot turns one sound into another.
1. start here: sweep left from the upper-right tip and shape the open head.
2. continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting.
3. lift once, then place the upper dot last — and only now lift.
Pen lifts: 1.

Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Introduction to Arabic: Egyptian Arabic for first-year students, Alphabet ع غ (ghayn), independent Ghayn at 00:02.4–00:04.0 (University of Oregon Libraries Open Textbook, 2023; accessed 2026-08-23).

segments.instruction: at إلى الغد and point at غ (ghayn) inside it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at **إلى الغد** and point at غ inside it]

segments.instruction: غ (ghayn) three times, saying gh as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: غ three times, saying *gh* as you finish each one]
[YOU WRITE: ز, then غ, from memory]

segments.text: Which letter is this — غ? (ghayn, gh.) Which word did it come from? (إلى الغد, ilā l-ghad, "see you tomorrow".)
